claim: HCV infections are on the rise in the United States, reflecting increasing rates of opioid addiction.
source: HCV infections are on the rise in the United States, reflecting increasing rates of opioid addiction (Zibbell et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zibbell et al., 2018

claim: An HCV vaccine is urgently needed to control the epidemic.
source: An HCV vaccine is urgently needed to control the epidemic, but vaccine development is challenging due to the enormous genetic diversity of the HCV envelope proteins (Yusim et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yusim et al., 2010 regarding genetic diversity challenge

claim: HCV vaccine development is challenging due to the enormous genetic diversity of the HCV envelope proteins.
source: An HCV vaccine is urgently needed to control the epidemic, but vaccine development is challenging due to the enormous genetic diversity of the HCV envelope proteins (Yusim et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yusim et al., 2010

claim: The HCV genome encodes two structural proteins, E1 and E2, that associate to form a noncovalent heterodimer, E1E2.
source: The HCV genome encodes two structural proteins, E1 and E2, that associate to form a noncovalent heterodimer, E1E2 (Freedman et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Freedman et al., 2016

claim: Potent bNAbs isolated from HCV-infected individuals predominantly target conserved epitopes in the front layer of the E2 glycoprotein.
source: Potent bNAbs isolated from HCV-infected individuals predominantly target conserved epitopes in the front layer of the E2 glycoprotein.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge in the field

claim: The majority of bNAbs that bind to the front layer are derived from VH1-69 genes.
source: The majority of bNAbs that bind to the front layer are derived from VH1-69 genes (Tzarum et al., 2019), which are also associated with bNAbs that target conserved epitopes on influenza virus and HIV-1 envelope glycoproteins (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tzarum et al., 2019

claim: VH1-69 genes are associated with bNAbs that target conserved epitopes on influenza virus and HIV-1 envelope glycoproteins.
source: The majority of bNAbs that bind to the front layer are derived from VH1-69 genes (Tzarum et al., 2019), which are also associated with bNAbs that target conserved epitopes on influenza virus and HIV-1 envelope glycoproteins (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2019

claim: HEPC3 and HEPC74 bNAbs were isolated from individuals who spontaneously cleared HCV infection.
source: We recently described crystal structures of two VH1-69 bNAbs, HEPC3 and HEPC74, isolated from individuals who spontaneously cleared HCV infection (Flyak et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Flyak et al., 2018

claim: HEPC3 and HEPC74 bNAbs utilized a disulfide motif in their CDRH3 regions to recognize a conserved epitope in the front layer of E2.
source: Both bNAbs utilized a disulfide motif in their CDRH3 regions to recognize a conserved epitope in the front layer of E2.
evidence: Supported by citation to Flyak et al., 2018 in the preceding sentence

claim: The HEPC3 and HEPC74 CDRH3 loops adopted a straight ß-hairpin conformation.
source: While the HEPC3 and HEPC74 CDRH3 loops adopted a straight ß-hairpin conformation, the VH1-69-encoded AR3A and AR3C bNAbs that were isolated from an individual with a chronic HCV infection included bent CDRH3 loops that contained an analogous disulfide motif (Kong et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kong et al., 2013 for comparison

claim: AR3A and AR3C bNAbs were isolated from an individual with a chronic HCV infection.
source: While the HEPC3 and HEPC74 CDRH3 loops adopted a straight ß-hairpin conformation, the VH1-69-encoded AR3A and AR3C bNAbs that were isolated from an individual with a chronic HCV infection included bent CDRH3 loops that contained an analogous disulfide motif (Kong et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kong et al., 2013

claim: AR3A and AR3C bNAbs included bent CDRH3 loops that contained an analogous disulfide motif.
source: While the HEPC3 and HEPC74 CDRH3 loops adopted a straight ß-hairpin conformation, the VH1-69-encoded AR3A and AR3C bNAbs that were isolated from an individual with a chronic HCV infection included bent CDRH3 loops that contained an analogous disulfide motif (Kong et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kong et al., 2013

claim: AR3X is a VH1-69-encoded antibody that included a CDRH3 with a disulfide motif and an unusually long 14-amino acid-long insertion in CDRH2.
source: Among bNAbs isolated from a chronically-infected individual (Law et al., 2008), we found AR3X, a VH1-69-encoded antibody that included a CDRH3 with a disulfide motif and an unusually long 14-amino acid-long insertion in CDRH2 (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citation to Law et al., 2008 and reference to Figure 1A

claim: The most likely scenario resulting in the insertion into the CDRH2 of AR3X involves a duplication event.
source: The most likely scenario resulting in the insertion into the CDRH2 of AR3X involves a duplication event, as the CDRH2 insertion has 69% identity with the N-terminal sequence preceding the CDRH2 (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by sequence identity data shown in Figure 1B

claim: The CDRH2 insertion has 69% identity with the N-terminal sequence preceding the CDRH2.
source: The most likely scenario resulting in the insertion into the CDRH2 of AR3X involves a duplication event, as the CDRH2 insertion has 69% identity with the N-terminal sequence preceding the CDRH2 (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1B

claim: The cysteines in the AR3X CDRH3 region are encoded by the human D gene segment 15 (IGHD2-15).
source: Similar to other front layer-specific bNAbs with the CDRH3 disulfide motif (Figure 1E), the cysteines in the AR3X CDRH3 region are encoded by the human D gene segment 15 (IGHD2-15) (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1C

claim: The C-terminal portion of the AR3X CDRH3 is likely encoded by human J-gene segment 3*02 (J3*02).
source: The C-terminal portion of the AR3X CDRH3 is likely encoded by human J-gene segment 3*02 (J3*02).
evidence: Based on inference from sequence analysis

claim: Not including the 14-amino acid insertion in CDRH2, AR3X shares 91% nucleotide identity with the VH1-69 gene segment and includes 17 somatic mutations.
source: Not including the 14-amino acid insertion in CDRH2, AR3X shares 91% nucleotide identity with the VH1-69 gene segment and includes 17 somatic mutations (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1D

claim: AR3X recognized all 19 E2 envelopes from genotype 1 including the 1a116 strain.
source: AR3X recognized all 19 E2 envelopes from genotype 1 including the 1a116 strain, which was not recognized by other front layer-specific bNAbs that include the CDRH3 disulfide motif (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Flyak et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by binding data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: The 1a116 strain was not recognized by other front layer-specific bNAbs that include the CDRH3 disulfide motif.
source: AR3X recognized all 19 E2 envelopes from genotype 1 including the 1a116 strain, which was not recognized by other front layer-specific bNAbs that include the CDRH3 disulfide motif (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Flyak et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Flyak et al., 2018 and data in Figure 2A

claim: AR3X recognized E2 envelopes from genotypes 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6.
source: AR3X also recognized E2 envelopes from genotypes 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by binding data shown in Figure 2A

claim: AR3X ΔINS protein that lacks the CDRH2 insertion bound only 4 of the 25 variants.
source: In contrast to mature AR3X, the AR3X ΔINS protein that lacks the CDRH2 insertion bound only 4 of the 25 variants, indicating that the CDRH2 insertion mediates the breath of binding.
evidence: Supported by binding data comparing AR3X and AR3X ΔINS

claim: The CDRH2 insertion mediates the breadth of binding of AR3X.
source: In contrast to mature AR3X, the AR3X ΔINS protein that lacks the CDRH2 insertion bound only 4 of the 25 variants, indicating that the CDRH2 insertion mediates the breath of binding.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of binding data between AR3X and AR3X ΔINS

claim: AR3Xrua failed to bind any E2ecto proteins.
source: While AR3Xrua failed to bind any E2ecto proteins, AR3Xrua + INS recognized 1 of the 25 variants, further highlighting the importance of the CDRH2 insertion in initial recognition of the E2 antigen by naïve B cells.
evidence: Supported by binding data for AR3Xrua

claim: AR3Xrua + INS recognized 1 of the 25 variants.
source: While AR3Xrua failed to bind any E2ecto proteins, AR3Xrua + INS recognized 1 of the 25 variants, further highlighting the importance of the CDRH2 insertion in initial recognition of the E2 antigen by naïve B cells.
evidence: Supported by binding data for AR3Xrua + INS

claim: The CDRH2 insertion is important for initial recognition of the E2 antigen by naïve B cells.
source: While AR3Xrua failed to bind any E2ecto proteins, AR3Xrua + INS recognized 1 of the 25 variants, further highlighting the importance of the CDRH2 insertion in initial recognition of the E2 antigen by naïve B cells.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of AR3Xrua and AR3Xrua + INS binding data

claim: Somatic mutations, in addition to the CDRH2 insertion, are required for breadth of binding and optimal E2 recognition.
source: The fact that AR3Xrua + INS only bound to one HCV strain, whereas mature AR3X recognized all strains, indicated that somatic mutations, in addition to the CDRH2 insertion, are required for breath of binding and optimal E2 recognition.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of binding data between AR3Xrua + INS and mature AR3X

claim: AR3X and two AR3X variants (AR3X ΔINS, AR3Xrua + INS) bound to 1a157.
source: Consistent with our previous studies in which the strain 1a157 E2ecto envelope was recognized by HEPC3, HEPC74, AR3C and their germline precursors (Flyak et al., 2018), AR3X and two AR3X variants (AR3X ΔINS, AR3Xrua + INS) also bound to 1a157, suggesting that immunogens based on the genotype 1 1a157 ectodomain sequence could be used to stimulate the development of potent front layer-specific bNAbs (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by binding data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Immunogens based on the genotype 1 1a157 ectodomain sequence could be used to stimulate the development of potent front layer-specific bNAbs.
source: Consistent with our previous studies in which the strain 1a157 E2ecto envelope was recognized by HEPC3, HEPC74, AR3C and their germline precursors (Flyak et al., 2018), AR3X and two AR3X variants (AR3X ΔINS, AR3Xrua + INS) also bound to 1a157, suggesting that immunogens based on the genotype 1 1a157 ectodomain sequence could be used to stimulate the development of potent front layer-specific bNAbs (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Speculative suggestion based on binding data and citation to Flyak et al., 2018

claim: Only mature AR3X exhibited neutralization activity, neutralizing 17 of 19 HCV strains.
source: Only mature AR3X exhibited neutralization activity, neutralizing 17 of 19 HCV strains (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by neutralization data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: The neutralization breadth of AR3X (89%) was slightly lower than the breadth of AR3C bNAb (100%).
source: The neutralization breadth of AR3X (89%) was slightly lower than the breath of AR3C bNAb (100%) (Flyak et al., 2018), which was isolated from the same HCV-infected individual (Law et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by neutralization data and citations to Flyak et al., 2018 and Law et al., 2008

claim: AR3C was isolated from the same HCV-infected individual as AR3X.
source: The neutralization breadth of AR3X (89%) was slightly lower than the breath of AR3C bNAb (100%) (Flyak et al., 2018), which was isolated from the same HCV-infected individual (Law et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Law et al., 2008

claim: AR3X variants failed to neutralize HCV isolates.
source: AR3X variants failed to neutralize HCV isolates, suggesting that both the CDRH2 insertion and somatic mutations are required for the broad neutralization activity of AR3X.
evidence: Supported by neutralization data for AR3X variants

claim: Both the CDRH2 insertion and somatic mutations are required for the broad neutralization activity of AR3X.
source: AR3X variants failed to neutralize HCV isolates, suggesting that both the CDRH2 insertion and somatic mutations are required for the broad neutralization activity of AR3X.
evidence: Inferred from neutralization data comparing AR3X and its variants

claim: The crystal structure of AR3X in complex with E2ecto from the 1b09 HCV strain was determined at 2.2 Å resolution.
source: To determine to which class AR3X belongs, we determined the crystal structure of AR3X in complex with E2ecto from the 1b09 HCV strain (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1). The 2.2 Å AR3X-E2ecto structure demonstrated that, similar to previously-characterized HCV bNAbs that recognize the neutralizing face of E2 (Flyak et al., 2018; Kong et al., 2013; Tzarum et al., 2019), AR3X binds to the conserved epitope in the E2 front layer (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: AR3X binds to the conserved epitope in the E2 front layer.
source: The 2.2 Å AR3X-E2ecto structure demonstrated that, similar to previously-characterized HCV bNAbs that recognize the neutralizing face of E2 (Flyak et al., 2018; Kong et al., 2013; Tzarum et al., 2019), AR3X binds to the conserved epitope in the E2 front layer (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 4A and citations

claim: The AR3X CDRH3 loop contains two cysteines that form a disulfide bond.
source: The AR3X CDRH3 loop contains two cysteines that form a disulfide bond, as seen in multiple other E2 front layer-binding bNAbs, and the AR3X CDRH3 adopts the straight conformation we previously described in the HEPC3 and HEPC74 bNAbs that were isolated from an individual who cleared HCV infection (Flyak et al., 2018; Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 3 and citation to Flyak et al., 2018

claim: The AR3X CDRH3 adopts the straight conformation previously described in the HEPC3 and HEPC74 bNAbs.
source: The AR3X CDRH3 loop contains two cysteines that form a disulfide bond, as seen in multiple other E2 front layer-binding bNAbs, and the AR3X CDRH3 adopts the straight conformation we previously described in the HEPC3 and HEPC74 bNAbs that were isolated from an individual who cleared HCV infection (Flyak et al., 2018; Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 3 and citation to Flyak et al., 2018

claim: The CDRH3s of AR3A and AR3C are bent.
source: By contrast, the CDRH3s of AR3A and AR3C, which were isolated from the same HCV-infected individual as AR3X (Law et al., 2008), are bent (Kong et al., 2013; Tzarum et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kong et al., 2013 and Tzarum et al., 2019

claim: AR3A and AR3C were isolated from the same HCV-infected individual as AR3X.
source: By contrast, the CDRH3s of AR3A and AR3C, which were isolated from the same HCV-infected individual as AR3X (Law et al., 2008), are bent (Kong et al., 2013; Tzarum et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Law et al., 2008

claim: The tip of the AR3X CDRH3 loop interacts with the same conserved residues in the front layer of E2 as the CDRH3 tips in the other HCV bNAbs.
source: The tip of the AR3X CDRH3 loop interacts with the same conserved residues in the front layer of E2 as the CDRH3 tips in the other HCV bNAbs (Figure 4e, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 4e and Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: AR3X has a similar binding footprint to the footprints of HEPC3, HEPC74, AR3C, and AR3A, sharing multiple contact residues in the front layer and CD81 receptor-binding loop.
source: Overall, AR3X has a similar binding footprint to the footprints of HEPC3, HEPC74, AR3C, and AR3A, sharing multiple contact residues in the front layer and CD81 receptor-binding loop (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: AR3X's contacts with E2ecto almost exclusively involved VH domain residues, burying 1,250 Å2 (98% of the total Fab buried surface area).
source: As also found for these other front layer-specific bNAbs, AR3X's contacts with E2ecto almost exclusively involved VH domain residues, burying 1,250 Å2 (98% of the total Fab buried surface area; BSA) (Figure 4B), with the CDRH3 accounting for 44.5% (556 Å2) of the total BSA on the VH domain (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by buried surface area calculations shown in Figure 4B

claim: The CDRH3 accounts for 44.5% (556 Å2) of the total BSA on the VH domain.
source: As also found for these other front layer-specific bNAbs, AR3X's contacts with E2ecto almost exclusively involved VH domain residues, burying 1,250 Å2 (98% of the total Fab buried surface area; BSA) (Figure 4B), with the CDRH3 accounting for 44.5% (556 Å2) of the total BSA on the VH domain (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by buried surface area calculations shown in Figure 4B

claim: The main contributor to the AR3X-E2ecto binding interface was CDRH2, which accounted for 48.2% (602 Å2) of the total BSA of the VH domain.
source: However, in contrast to other front layer-specific bNAbs in which the CDRH3 plays a dominant role in the interactions with E2 envelope (Flyak et al., 2018; Kong et al., 2013; Tzarum et al., 2019), the main contributor to the AR3X-E2ecto binding interface was CDRH2, which accounted for 48.2% (602 Å2) of the total BSA of the VH domain, with the majority of the binding footprint provided by the CDRH2 insertion (45.4% or 567 Å2 of total BSA of the VH domain) (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by buried surface area calculations shown in Figure 4C

claim: The majority of the binding footprint was provided by the CDRH2 insertion (45.4% or 567 Å2 of total BSA of the VH domain).
source: However, in contrast to other front layer-specific bNAbs in which the CDRH3 plays a dominant role in the interactions with E2 envelope (Flyak et al., 2018; Kong et al., 2013; Tzarum et al., 2019), the main contributor to the AR3X-E2ecto binding interface was CDRH2, which accounted for 48.2% (602 Å2) of the total BSA of the VH domain, with the majority of the binding footprint provided by the CDRH2 insertion (45.4% or 567 Å2 of total BSA of the VH domain) (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by buried surface area calculations shown in Figure 4C

claim: AR3X has an unusually long 42-nucleotide insertion, which results in a 31-residue CDRH2.
source: While the size of an insertion or deletion in human antibody genes ranges from 3 to 33 nucleotides (Kanyavuz et al., 2019), AR3X has a unusually long 42-nucleotide insertion, which results in a 31-residue CDRH2 (Kabat definition: [Kabat and National Institutes of Health (U.S.). Office of the Director, 1991]).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kanyavuz et al., 2019 and Kabat definition

claim: A typical human CDRH2 is 17 residues (relative frequency 67%).
source: According to the abYsis database (Swindells et al., 2017), a typical human CDRH2 is 17 residues (relative frequency 67%) (Figure 4D), and CDRH2s longer than 20 residues are rare (relative frequency <1%).
evidence: Supported by data from abYsis database cited as Swindells et al., 2017 and shown in Figure 4D

claim: CDRH2s longer than 20 residues are rare (relative frequency <1%).
source: According to the abYsis database (Swindells et al., 2017), a typical human CDRH2 is 17 residues (relative frequency 67%) (Figure 4D), and CDRH2s longer than 20 residues are rare (relative frequency <1%).
evidence: Supported by data from abYsis database cited as Swindells et al., 2017 and shown in Figure 4D

claim: AR3X with its 31-residue CDRH2 represents the longest CDRH2 among antibody structures available in the Protein Data Bank (PDB).
source: To our knowledge, AR3X with its 31-residue CDRH2 represents the longest CDRH2 among antibody structures available in the Protein Data Bank (PDB).
evidence: Based on knowledge of PDB structures at the time of writing

claim: AR3X CDRH2 contacts the C-terminus of the E2 α1-helix, the portion of the E2 front layer between the α-helix, variable region 2 (residues 446–448), and the back layer of E2 (residues 444, 445).
source: Although the CDH3s of AR3X, AR3A, AR3C, HEPC3, and HEPC74 CDRH3s make similar binding footprints on the E2 surface (Figure 5), the difference in Fab approach angles and the presence of the long insertion in the AR3X CDRH2 result in different footprints on E2 for the VH1-69–encoded CDRH2 loops of the bNAbs: AR3X CDRH2 contacts the C-terminus of the E2 α1-helix, the portion of the E2 front layer between the α-helix, variable region 2 (residues 446–448), and the back layer of E2 (residues 444, 445) (Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: The AR3A and AR3C CDRH2 contacts are reduced to hydrophobic residues in α1-helix.
source: In contrast, the AR3A and AR3C CDRH2 contacts are reduced to hydrophobic residues in α1-helix (Kong et al., 2013), whereas the HEPC3 and HEPC74 CDRH2s contact the E2 α1-helix and the portion of the E2 front layer between the α1-helix and variable region 2 (residues 446–448) (Flyak et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kong et al., 2013

claim: The HEPC3 and HEPC74 CDRH2s contact the E2 α1-helix and the portion of the E2 front layer between the α1-helix and variable region 2 (residues 446–448).
source: In contrast, the AR3A and AR3C CDRH2 contacts are reduced to hydrophobic residues in α1-helix (Kong et al., 2013), whereas the HEPC3 and HEPC74 CDRH2s contact the E2 α1-helix and the portion of the E2 front layer between the α1-helix and variable region 2 (residues 446–448) (Flyak et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Flyak et al., 2018

claim: A feature of VH1-69-derived antibodies is the presence of two hydrophobic residues at the tip of the CDRH2 loop that facilitate interactions with hydrophobic epitopes.
source: A feature of VH1-69-derived antibodies is the presence of two hydrophobic residues at the tip of the CDRH2 loop that facilitate interactions with hydrophobic epitopes.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of VH1-69 antibodies

claim: The CDRH2s of AR3A and AR3C contain an Ile/Val-Pro-Met/Leu-Phe motif in which hydrophobic residues interact with the E2 front layer and CD81 binding loop.
source: The CDRH2s of AR3A and AR3C contain an Ile/Val-Pro-Met/Leu-Phe motif in which hydrophobic residues interact with the E2 front layer and CD81 binding loop (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2019

claim: The CDRH2s of HEPC3 and HEPC74 are less hydrophobic and contain a Thr/Ser-Pro-Ile-Phe/Ser motif.
source: The CDRH2s of HEPC3 and HEPC74 are less hydrophobic and contain a Thr/Ser-Pro-Ile-Phe/Ser motif (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2019

claim: The HEPC3 CDRH2 makes a single hydrogen bond with E2.
source: In addition to hydrophobic interactions with the E2 front layer, the HEPC3 CDRH2 also makes a single hydrogen bond with E2 (Flyak et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Flyak et al., 2018

claim: AR3X is not a typical VH1-69 antibody in which hydrophobic residues in CDRH2 mediate the binding to hydrophobic residues in E2.
source: By contrast, AR3X is a not a typical VH1-69 antibody in which hydrophobic residues in CDRH2 mediate the binding to hydrophobic residues in E2 (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2019 for comparison

claim: The AR3X CDRH2 forms eight hydrogen bonds with the E2 glycoprotein.
source: Instead, the AR3X CDRH2 forms eight hydrogen bonds with the E2 glycoprotein, four of which are mediated by AR3X residue Arg52g (AR3X-E2ecto: Pro52c-His445, Pro52e-Thr444, Arg52g-Ala440, Arg52g-Phe442, Arg52g-Tyr443, Arg52g-Pro612, Asn52n-Tyr443, Trp52i-Tyr613) (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: Four of the eight hydrogen bonds between AR3X CDRH2 and E2 are mediated by AR3X residue Arg52g.
source: Instead, the AR3X CDRH2 forms eight hydrogen bonds with the E2 glycoprotein, four of which are mediated by AR3X residue Arg52g (AR3X-E2ecto: Pro52c-His445, Pro52e-Thr444, Arg52g-Ala440, Arg52g-Phe442, Arg52g-Tyr443, Arg52g-Pro612, Asn52n-Tyr443, Trp52i-Tyr613) (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: The AR3X neutralization IC50 for strain 1b21 is ~17 fold lower than the IC50 of HEPC3 (1.2 vs. 20.5 µg/mL).
source: Notably, these differences in binding interactions have functional implications, as these mAbs differ in potency of neutralization of individual HCV strains in the HCVpp panel. For example, the AR3X neutralization IC50 for strain 1b21 is ~17 fold lower than the IC50 of HEPC3 (1.2 vs. 20.5 µg/mL).
evidence: Supported by neutralization data from Figure 2 and Flyak et al., 2018

claim: The AR3X neutralization IC50 for strain 1a142 is ~9 fold higher than the IC50 of HEPC3 (16.2 vs. 1.9 µg/mL).
source: In contrast, the AR3X neutralization IC50 for strain 1a142 is ~9 fold higher than the IC50 of HEPC3 (16.2 vs. 1.9 µg/mL) (Figure 2; Flyak et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by neutralization data from Figure 2 and citation to Flyak et al., 2018

claim: The first cysteine residue of the AR3X CDRH3 (Cys100a) hydrogen bonds with E2 residue Cys429.
source: Similar to other front layer-specific bNAbs with a CDRH3 disulfide motif, the first cysteine residue of the AR3X CDRH3 (Cys100a) hydrogen bonds with E2 residue Cys429 (Figure 4G, Figure 4—figure supplement 2; Flyak et al., 2018; Kong et al., 2013; Tzarum et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 2, and citations

claim: Three additional hydrogen bonds (AR3X-E2ecto: Arg99-Asp431, Arg99-Asn430, Asn96-Asp431) stabilize the interaction of AR3X with E2.
source: Three additional hydrogen bonds (AR3X-E2ecto: Arg99-Asp431, Arg99-Asn430, Asn96-Asp431), as well as a salt bridge between CDRH3 (Arg100b) and a CD81 binding loop residue (Glu531), further stabilize the interaction of AR3X with E2.
evidence: Supported by structural data

claim: A salt bridge between CDRH3 (Arg100b) and a CD81 binding loop residue (Glu531) stabilizes the interaction of AR3X with E2.
source: Three additional hydrogen bonds (AR3X-E2ecto: Arg99-Asp431, Arg99-Asn430, Asn96-Asp431), as well as a salt bridge between CDRH3 (Arg100b) and a CD81 binding loop residue (Glu531), further stabilize the interaction of AR3X with E2.
evidence: Supported by structural data

claim: The AR3X-E2ecto crystal structure shows contacts between the AR3X CDRH3 and N-glycans attached to E2 residues Asn423 and Asn430.
source: The AR3X-E2ecto crystal structure also shows contacts between the AR3X CDRH3 and N-glycans attached to E2 residues Asn423 and Asn430 (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 4G

claim: A single individual can produce potent HCV-specific bNAbs using the common VH1-69 and D2-15 genes that bind to the conserved region of E2 in at least three different configurations.
source: This indicates that a single individual can produce potent HCV-specific bNAbs using the common VH1-69 and D2-15 genes that bind to the conserved region of E2 in at least three different configurations (straight CDRH3 with CDRH2 insertion, straight CDRH3 without CDRH2 insertion, or bent CDRH3 without CDRH2 insertion), highlighting the intrinsic plasticity of the VH1-69–encoded CDRH1 and CDRH2 loops that accommodate different antibody approach angles (Figure 5).
evidence: Inferred from structural comparison of AR3X, AR3A, AR3C from the same individual, shown in Figure 5

claim: The intrinsic plasticity of the VH1-69–encoded CDRH1 and CDRH2 loops accommodates different antibody approach angles.
source: This indicates that a single individual can produce potent HCV-specific bNAbs using the common VH1-69 and D2-15 genes that bind to the conserved region of E2 in at least three different configurations (straight CDRH3 with CDRH2 insertion, straight CDRH3 without CDRH2 insertion, or bent CDRH3 without CDRH2 insertion), highlighting the intrinsic plasticity of the VH1-69–encoded CDRH1 and CDRH2 loops that accommodate different antibody approach angles (Figure 5).
evidence: Inferred from structural comparison shown in Figure 5

claim: The CDRH3s of these bNAbs likely dictate the preferential mode of engagement of bNAb germline precursors with the conserved epitope in the E2 front layer.
source: It's likely that the CDRH3s of these bNAbs dictate the preferential mode of engagement of bNAb germline precursors with the conserved epitope in the E2 front layer.
evidence: Speculative inference based on structural observations

claim: B cells using VH1-69 and D2-15 genes can follow multiple pathways of affinity maturation to achieve broad neutralizing activity.
